speeches.speaker: PROLOGUE
speeches.text: Excuse me, sirs, I pray—I can’t yet speak— I’m crying now—and have been all the week. “’Tis not alone this mourning suit,” good masters: “I’ve that within”—for which there are no plasters! Pray, would you know the reason why I’m crying? The Comic Muse, long sick, is now a-dying! And if she goes, my tears will never stop; For as a player, I can’t squeeze out one drop: I am undone, that’s all—shall lose my bread— I’d rather, but that’s nothing—lose my head. When the sweet maid is laid upon the bier, Shuter and I shall be chief mourners here. To her a mawkish drab of spurious breed, Who deals in sentimentals, will succeed! Poor Ned and I are dead to all intents; We can as soon speak Greek as sentiments! Both nervous grown, to keep our spirits up. We now and then take down a hearty cup. What shall we do? If Comedy forsake us, They’ll turn us out, and no one else will take us. But why can’t I be moral?—Let me try— My heart thus pressing—fixed my face and eye— With a sententious look, that nothing means, (Faces are blocks in sentimental scenes) Thus I begin: “All is not gold that glitters, “Pleasure seems sweet, but proves a glass of bitters. “When Ignorance enters, Folly is at hand: “Learning is better far than house and land. “Let not your virtue trip; who trips may stumble, “And virtue is not virtue, if she tumble.” I give it up—morals won’t do for me; To make you laugh, I must play tragedy. One hope remains—hearing the maid was ill, A Doctor comes this night to show his skill. To cheer her heart, and give your muscles motion, He, in Five Draughts prepar’d, presents a potion: A kind of magic charm—for be assur’d, If you will swallow it, the maid is cur’d: But desperate the Doctor, and her case is, If you reject the dose, and make wry faces! This truth he boasts, will boast it while he lives, No poisonous drugs are mixed in what he gives. Should he succeed, you’ll give him his degree; If not, within he will receive no fee! The College YOU, must his pretensions back, Pronounce him Regular, or dub him Quack.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I vow, Mr. Hardcastle, you’re very particular. Is there a creature in the whole country but ourselves, that does not take a trip to town now and then, to rub off the rust a little? There’s the two Miss Hoggs, and our neighbour Mrs. Grigsby, go to take a month’s polishing every winter.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, and bring back vanity and affectation to last them the whole year. I wonder why London cannot keep its own fools at home! In my time, the follies of the town crept slowly among us, but now they travel faster than a stage-coach. Its fopperies come down not only as inside passengers, but in the very basket.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, your times were fine times indeed; you have been telling us of them for many a long year. Here we live in an old rumbling mansion, that looks for all the world like an inn, but that we never see company. Our best visitors are old Mrs. Oddfish, the curate’s wife, and little Cripplegate, the lame dancing-master; and all our entertainment your old stories of Prince Eugene and the Duke of Marlborough. I hate such old-fashioned trumpery.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And I love it. I love everything that’s old: old friends, old times, old manners, old books, old wine; and I believe, Dorothy, you’ll own I have been pretty fond of an old wife.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Lord, Mr. Hardcastle, you’re for ever at your Dorothys and your old wifes. You may be a Darby, but I’ll be no Joan, I promise you. I’m not so old as you’d make me, by more than one good year. Add twenty to twenty, and make money of that.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Let me see; twenty added to twenty makes just fifty and seven.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: It’s false, Mr. Hardcastle; I was but twenty when I was brought to bed of Tony, that I had by Mr. Lumpkin, my first husband; and he’s not come to years of discretion yet.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Nor ever will, I dare answer for him. Ay, you have taught him finely.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: No matter. Tony Lumpkin has a good fortune. My son is not to live by his learning. I don’t think a boy wants much learning to spend fifteen hundred a year.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Learning, quotha! a mere composition of tricks and mischief.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Humour, my dear; nothing but humour. Come, Mr. Hardcastle, you must allow the boy a little humour.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I’d sooner allow him a horse-pond. If burning the footmen’s shoes, frightening the maids, and worrying the kittens be humour, he has it. It was but yesterday he fastened my wig to the back of my chair, and when I went to make a bow, I popt my bald head in Mrs. Frizzle’s face.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And am I to blame? The poor boy was always too sickly to do any good. A school would be his death. When he comes to be a little stronger, who knows what a year or two’s Latin may do for him?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Latin for him! A cat and fiddle. No, no; the alehouse and the stable are the only schools he’ll ever go to.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, we must not snub the poor boy now, for I believe we shan’t have him long among us. Anybody that looks in his face may see he’s consumptive.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, if growing too fat be one of the symptoms.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: He coughs sometimes.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Yes, when his liquor goes the wrong way.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I’m actually afraid of his lungs.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And truly so am I; for he sometimes whoops like a speaking trumpet— —O, there he goes—a very consumptive figure, truly.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Tony, where are you going, my charmer? Won’t you give papa and I a little of your company, lovee?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I’m in haste, mother; I cannot stay.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You shan’t venture out this raw evening, my dear; you look most shockingly.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I can’t stay, I tell you. The Three Pigeons expects me down every moment. There’s some fun going forward.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay; the alehouse, the old place: I thought so.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: A low, paltry set of fellows.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Not so low, neither. There’s Dick Muggins the exciseman, Jack Slang the horse doctor, Little Aminadab that grinds the music box, and Tom Twist that spins the pewter platter.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Pray, my dear, disappoint them for one night at least.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: As for disappointing them, I should not so much mind; but I can’t abide to disappoint myself.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You shan’t go.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I will, I tell you.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I say you shan’t.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: We’ll see which is strongest, you or I.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, there goes a pair that only spoil each other. But is not the whole age in a combination to drive sense and discretion out of doors? There’s my pretty darling Kate! the fashions of the times have almost infected her too. By living a year or two in town, she is as fond of gauze and French frippery as the best of them.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Blessings on my pretty innocence! drest out as usual, my Kate. Goodness! What a quantity of superfluous silk hast thou got about thee, girl! I could never teach the fools of this age, that the indigent world could be clothed out of the trimmings of the vain.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You know our agreement, sir. You allow me the morning to receive and pay visits, and to dress in my own manner; and in the evening I put on my housewife’s dress to please you.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, remember, I insist on the terms of our agreement; and, by the bye, I believe I shall have occasion to try your obedience this very evening.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I protest, sir, I don’t comprehend your meaning.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Then to be plain with you, Kate, I expect the young gentleman I have chosen to be your husband from town this very day. I have his father’s letter, in which he informs me his son is set out, and that he intends to follow himself shortly after.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Indeed! I wish I had known something of this before. Bless me, how shall I behave? It’s a thousand to one I shan’t like him; our meeting will be so formal, and so like a thing of business, that I shall find no room for friendship or esteem.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Depend upon it, child, I’ll never control your choice; but Mr. Marlow, whom I have pitched upon, is the son of my old friend, Sir Charles Marlow, of whom you have heard me talk so often. The young gentleman has been bred a scholar, and is designed for an employment in the service of his country. I am told he’s a man of an excellent understanding.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Is he?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Very generous.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I believe I shall like him.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Young and brave.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I’m sure I shall like him.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And very handsome.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: My dear papa, say no more,, he’s mine; I’ll have him.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And, to crown all, Kate, he’s one of the most bashful and reserved young fellows in all the world.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Eh! you have frozen me to death again. That word RESERVED has undone all the rest of his accomplishments. A reserved lover, it is said, always makes a suspicious husband.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: On the contrary, modesty seldom resides in a breast that is not enriched with nobler virtues. It was the very feature in his character that first struck me.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: He must have more striking features to catch me, I promise you. However, if he be so young, so handsome, and so everything as you mention, I believe he’ll do still. I think I’ll have him.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, Kate, but there is still an obstacle. It’s more than an even wager he may not have you.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: My dear papa, why will you mortify one so?—Well, if he refuses, instead of breaking my heart at his indifference, I’ll only break my glass for its flattery, set my cap to some newer fashion, and look out for some less difficult admirer.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Bravely resolved! In the mean time I’ll go prepare the servants for his reception: as we seldom see company, they want as much training as a company of recruits the first day’s muster.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Lud, this news of papa’s puts me all in a flutter. Young, handsome: these he put last; but I put them foremost. Sensible, good-natured; I like all that. But then reserved and sheepish; that’s much against him. Yet can’t he be cured of his timidity, by being taught to be proud of his wife? Yes, and can’t I—But I vow I’m disposing of the husband before I have secured the lover.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I’m glad you’re come, Neville, my dear. Tell me, Constance, how do I look this evening? Is there anything whimsical about me? Is it one of my well-looking days, child? Am I in face to-day?

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Perfectly, my dear. Yet now I look again—bless me!—sure no accident has happened among the canary birds or the gold fishes. Has your brother or the cat been meddling? or has the last novel been too moving?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: No; nothing of all this. I have been threatened—I can scarce get it out—I have been threatened with a lover.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: And his name—

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Is Marlow.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Indeed!

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: The son of Sir Charles Marlow.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: As I live, the most intimate friend of Mr. Hastings, my admirer. They are never asunder. I believe you must have seen him when we lived in town.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Never.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: He’s a very singular character, I assure you. Among women of reputation and virtue he is the modestest man alive; but his acquaintance give him a very different character among creatures of another stamp: you understand me.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: An odd character indeed. I shall never be able to manage him. What shall I do? Pshaw, think no more of him, but trust to occurrences for success. But how goes on your own affair, my dear? has my mother been courting you for my brother Tony as usual?

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I have just come from one of our agreeable tete-a-tetes. She has been saying a hundred tender things, and setting off her pretty monster as the very pink of perfection.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And her partiality is such, that she actually thinks him so. A fortune like yours is no small temptation. Besides, as she has the sole management of it, I’m not surprised to see her unwilling to let it go out of the family.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: A fortune like mine, which chiefly consists in jewels, is no such mighty temptation. But at any rate, if my dear Hastings be but constant, I make no doubt to be too hard for her at last. However, I let her suppose that I am in love with her son; and she never once dreams that my affections are fixed upon another.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: My good brother holds out stoutly. I could almost love him for hating you so.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: It is a good-natured creature at bottom, and I’m sure would wish to see me married to anybody but himself. But my aunt’s bell rings for our afternoon’s walk round the improvements. Allons! Courage is necessary, as our affairs are critical.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: “Would it were bed-time, and all were well.”

speeches.speaker: OMNES
speeches.text: Hurrea! hurrea! hurrea! bravo!

speeches.speaker: FIRST FELLOW
speeches.text: Now, gentlemen, silence for a song. The ’squire is going to knock himself down for a song.

speeches.speaker: OMNES
speeches.text: Ay, a song, a song!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Then I’ll sing you, gentlemen, a song I made upon this alehouse, the Three Pigeons. Let schoolmasters puzzle their brain With grammar, and nonsense, and learning, Good liquor, I stoutly maintain, Gives GENUS a better discerning. Let them brag of their heathenish gods, Their Lethes, their Styxes, and Stygians, Their Quis, and their Quaes, and their Quods, They’re all but a parcel of Pigeons. Toroddle, toroddle, toroll. When methodist preachers come down, A-preaching that drinking is sinful, I’ll wager the rascals a crown, They always preach best with a skinful. But when you come down with your pence, For a slice of their scurvy religion, I’ll leave it to all men of sense, But you, my good friend, are the Pigeon. Toroddle, toroddle, toroll. Then come, put the jorum about, And let us be merry and clever, Our hearts and our liquors are stout, Here’s the Three Jolly Pigeons for ever. Let some cry up woodcock or hare, Your bustards, your ducks, and your widgeons; But of all the GAY birds in the air, Here’s a health to the Three Jolly Pigeons. Toroddle, toroddle, toroll.

speeches.speaker: OMNES
speeches.text: Bravo, bravo!

speeches.speaker: FIRST FELLOW
speeches.text: The ’squire has got spunk in him.

speeches.speaker: SECOND FELLOW
speeches.text: I loves to hear him sing, bekeays he never gives us nothing that’s low.

speeches.speaker: THIRD FELLOW
speeches.text: O damn anything that’s low, I cannot bear it.

speeches.speaker: FOURTH FELLOW
speeches.text: The genteel thing is the genteel thing any time: if so be that a gentleman bees in a concatenation accordingly.

speeches.speaker: THIRD FELLOW
speeches.text: I likes the maxum of it, Master Muggins. What, though I am obligated to dance a bear, a man may be a gentleman for all that. May this be my poison, if my bear ever dances but to the very genteelest of tunes; “Water Parted,” or “The minuet in Ariadne.”

speeches.speaker: SECOND FELLOW
speeches.text: What a pity it is the ’squire is not come to his own. It would be well for all the publicans within ten miles round of him.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ecod, and so it would, Master Slang. I’d then show what it was to keep choice of company.

speeches.speaker: SECOND FELLOW
speeches.text: O he takes after his own father for that. To be sure old ’Squire Lumpkin was the finest gentleman I ever set my eyes on. For winding the straight horn, or beating a thicket for a hare, or a wench, he never had his fellow. It was a saying in the place, that he kept the best horses, dogs, and girls, in the whole county.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ecod, and when I’m of age, I’ll be no bastard, I promise you. I have been thinking of Bet Bouncer and the miller’s grey mare to begin with. But come, my boys, drink about and be merry, for you pay no reckoning. Well, Stingo, what’s the matter?

speeches.speaker: LANDLORD
speeches.text: There be two gentlemen in a post-chaise at the door. They have lost their way upo’ the forest; and they are talking something about Mr. Hardcastle.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: As sure as can be, one of them must be the gentleman that’s coming down to court my sister. Do they seem to be Londoners?

speeches.speaker: LANDLORD
speeches.text: I believe they may. They look woundily like Frenchmen.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Then desire them to step this way, and I’ll set them right in a twinkling. Gentlemen, as they mayn’t be good enough company for you, step down for a moment, and I’ll be with you in the squeezing of a lemon.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Father-in-law has been calling me whelp and hound this half year. Now, if I pleased, I could be so revenged upon the old grumbletonian. But then I’m afraid—afraid of what? I shall soon be worth fifteen hundred a year, and let him frighten me out of THAT if he can.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: What a tedious uncomfortable day have we had of it! We were told it was but forty miles across the country, and we have come above threescore.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: And all, Marlow, from that unaccountable reserve of yours, that would not let us inquire more frequently on the way.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I own, Hastings, I am unwilling to lay myself under an obligation to every one I meet, and often stand the chance of an unmannerly answer.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: At present, however, we are not likely to receive any answer.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: No offence, gentlemen. But I’m told you have been inquiring for one Mr. Hardcastle in these parts. Do you know what part of the country you are in?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Not in the least, sir, but should thank you for information.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Nor the way you came?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: No, sir: but if you can inform us——

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Why, gentlemen, if you know neither the road you are going, nor where you are, nor the road you came, the first thing I have to inform you is, that—you have lost your way.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: We wanted no ghost to tell us that.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Pray, gentlemen, may I be so bold so as to ask the place from whence you came?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: That’s not necessary towards directing us where we are to go.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: No offence; but question for question is all fair, you know. Pray, gentlemen, is not this same Hardcastle a cross-grained, old-fashioned, whimsical fellow, with an ugly face, a daughter, and a pretty son?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: We have not seen the gentleman; but he has the family you mention.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: The daughter, a tall, trapesing, trolloping, talkative maypole; the son, a pretty, well-bred, agreeable youth, that everybody is fond of.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Our information differs in this. The daughter is said to be well-bred and beautiful; the son an awkward booby, reared up and spoiled at his mother’s apron-string.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: He-he-hem!—Then, gentlemen, all I have to tell you is, that you won’t reach Mr. Hardcastle’s house this night, I believe.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Unfortunate!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: It’s a damn’d long, dark, boggy, dirty, dangerous way. Stingo, tell the gentlemen the way to Mr. Hardcastle’s! Mr. Hardcastle’s, of Quagmire Marsh, you understand me.

speeches.speaker: LANDLORD
speeches.text: Master Hardcastle’s! Lock-a-daisy, my masters, you’re come a deadly deal wrong! When you came to the bottom of the hill, you should have crossed down Squash Lane.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Cross down Squash Lane!

speeches.speaker: LANDLORD
speeches.text: Then you were to keep straight forward, till you came to four roads.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Come to where four roads meet?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ay; but you must be sure to take only one of them.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: O, sir, you’re facetious.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Then keeping to the right, you are to go sideways till you come upon Crackskull Common: there you must look sharp for the track of the wheel, and go forward till you come to farmer Murrain’s barn. Coming to the farmer’s barn, you are to turn to the right, and then to the left, and then to the right about again, till you find out the old mill—

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Zounds, man! we could as soon find out the longitude!

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: What’s to be done, Marlow?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: This house promises but a poor reception; though perhaps the landlord can accommodate us.

speeches.speaker: LANDLORD
speeches.text: Alack, master, we have but one spare bed in the whole house.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: And to my knowledge, that’s taken up by three lodgers already. I have hit it. Don’t you think, Stingo, our landlady could accommodate the gentlemen by the fire-side, with——three chairs and a bolster?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: I hate sleeping by the fire-side.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: And I detest your three chairs and a bolster.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: You do, do you? then, let me see—what if you go on a mile further, to the Buck’s Head; the old Buck’s Head on the hill, one of the best inns in the whole county?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: O ho! so we have escaped an adventure for this night, however.

speeches.speaker: LANDLORD
speeches.text: Sure, you ben’t sending them to your father’s as an inn, be you?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Mum, you fool you. Let THEM find that out. You have only to keep on straight forward, till you come to a large old house by the road side. You’ll see a pair of large horns over the door. That’s the sign. Drive up the yard, and call stoutly about you.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Sir, we are obliged to you. The servants can’t miss the way?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: No, no: but I tell you, though, the landlord is rich, and going to leave off business; so he wants to be thought a gentleman, saving your presence, he! he! he! He’ll be for giving you his company; and, ecod, if you mind him, he’ll persuade you that his mother was an alderman, and his aunt a justice of peace.

speeches.speaker: LANDLORD
speeches.text: A troublesome old blade, to be sure; but a keeps as good wines and beds as any in the whole country.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Well, if he supplies us with these, we shall want no farther connexion. We are to turn to the right, did you say?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: No, no; straight forward. I’ll just step myself, and show you a piece of the way. Mum!

speeches.speaker: LANDLORD
speeches.text: Ah, bless your heart, for a sweet, pleasant—damn’d mischievous son of a whore.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, I hope you are perfect in the table exercise I have been teaching you these three days. You all know your posts and your places, and can show that you have been used to good company, without ever stirring from home.

speeches.speaker: OMNES
speeches.text: Ay, ay.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: When company comes you are not to pop out and stare, and then run in again, like frightened rabbits in a warren.

speeches.speaker: OMNES
speeches.text: No, no.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You, Diggory, whom I have taken from the barn, are to make a show at the side-table; and you, Roger, whom I have advanced from the plough, are to place yourself behind my chair. But you’re not to stand so, with your hands in your pockets. Take your hands from your pockets, Roger; and from your head, you blockhead you. See how Diggory carries his hands. They’re a little too stiff, indeed, but that’s no great matter.

speeches.speaker: DIGGORY
speeches.text: Ay, mind how I hold them. I learned to hold my hands this way when I was upon drill for the militia. And so being upon drill——

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You must not be so talkative, Diggory. You must be all attention to the guests. You must hear us talk, and not think of talking; you must see us drink, and not think of drinking; you must see us eat, and not think of eating.

speeches.speaker: DIGGORY
speeches.text: By the laws, your worship, that’s parfectly unpossible. Whenever Diggory sees yeating going forward, ecod, he’s always wishing for a mouthful himself.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Blockhead! Is not a belly-full in the kitchen as good as a belly-full in the parlour? Stay your stomach with that reflection.

speeches.speaker: DIGGORY
speeches.text: Ecod, I thank your worship, I’ll make a shift to stay my stomach with a slice of cold beef in the pantry.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Diggory, you are too talkative.—Then, if I happen to say a good thing, or tell a good story at table, you must not all burst out a-laughing, as if you made part of the company.

speeches.speaker: DIGGORY
speeches.text: Then ecod your worship must not tell the story of Ould Grouse in the gun-room: I can’t help laughing at that—he! he! he!—for the soul of me. We have laughed at that these twenty years—ha! ha! ha!

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ha! ha! ha! The story is a good one. Well, honest Diggory, you may laugh at that—but still remember to be attentive. Suppose one of the company should call for a glass of wine, how will you behave? A glass of wine, sir, if you please.—Eh, why don’t you move?

speeches.speaker: DIGGORY
speeches.text: Ecod, your worship, I never have courage till I see the eatables and drinkables brought upo’ the table, and then I’m as bauld as a lion.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: What, will nobody move?

speeches.speaker: FIRST SERVANT
speeches.text: I’m not to leave this pleace.

speeches.speaker: SECOND SERVANT
speeches.text: I’m sure it’s no pleace of mine.

speeches.speaker: THIRD SERVANT
speeches.text: Nor mine, for sartain.

speeches.speaker: DIGGORY
speeches.text: Wauns, and I’m sure it canna be mine.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You numskulls! and so while, like your betters, you are quarrelling for places, the guests must be starved. O you dunces! I find I must begin all over again——But don’t I hear a coach drive into the yard? To your posts, you blockheads. I’ll go in the mean time and give my old friend’s son a hearty reception at the gate.

speeches.speaker: DIGGORY
speeches.text: By the elevens, my pleace is gone quite out of my head.

speeches.speaker: ROGER
speeches.text: I know that my pleace is to be everywhere.

speeches.speaker: FIRST SERVANT
speeches.text: Where the devil is mine?

speeches.speaker: SECOND SERVANT
speeches.text: My pleace is to be nowhere at all; and so I’ze go about my business.

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
speeches.text: Welcome, gentlemen, very welcome! This way.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: After the disappointments of the day, welcome once more, Charles, to the comforts of a clean room and a good fire. Upon my word, a very well-looking house; antique but creditable.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: The usual fate of a large mansion. Having first ruined the master by good housekeeping, it at last comes to levy contributions as an inn.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: As you say, we passengers are to be taxed to pay all these fineries. I have often seen a good sideboard, or a marble chimney-piece, though not actually put in the bill, inflame a reckoning confoundedly.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Travellers, George, must pay in all places: the only difference is, that in good inns you pay dearly for luxuries; in bad inns you are fleeced and starved.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: You have lived very much among them. In truth, I have been often surprised, that you who have seen so much of the world, with your natural good sense, and your many opportunities, could never yet acquire a requisite share of assurance.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: The Englishman’s malady. But tell me, George, where could I have learned that assurance you talk of? My life has been chiefly spent in a college or an inn, in seclusion from that lovely part of the creation that chiefly teach men confidence. I don’t know that I was ever familiarly acquainted with a single modest woman—except my mother—But among females of another class, you know——

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Ay, among them you are impudent enough of all conscience.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: They are of US, you know.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But in the company of women of reputation I never saw such an idiot, such a trembler; you look for all the world as if you wanted an opportunity of stealing out of the room.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Why, man, that’s because I do want to steal out of the room. Faith, I have often formed a resolution to break the ice, and rattle away at any rate. But I don’t know how, a single glance from a pair of fine eyes has totally overset my resolution. An impudent fellow may counterfeit modesty; but I’ll be hanged if a modest man can ever counterfeit impudence.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: If you could but say half the fine things to them that I have heard you lavish upon the bar-maid of an inn, or even a college bed-maker——

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Why, George, I can’t say fine things to them; they freeze, they petrify me. They may talk of a comet, or a burning mountain, or some such bagatelle; but, to me, a modest woman, drest out in all her finery, is the most tremendous object of the whole creation.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Ha! ha! ha! At this rate, man, how can you ever expect to marry?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Never; unless, as among kings and princes, my bride were to be courted by proxy. If, indeed, like an Eastern bridegroom, one were to be introduced to a wife he never saw before, it might be endured. But to go through all the terrors of a formal courtship, together with the episode of aunts, grandmothers, and cousins, and at last to blurt out the broad staring question of, Madam, will you marry me? No, no, that’s a strain much above me, I assure you.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: I pity you. But how do you intend behaving to the lady you are come down to visit at the request of your father?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: As I behave to all other ladies. Bow very low, answer yes or no to all her demands—But for the rest, I don’t think I shall venture to look in her face till I see my father’s again.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: I’m surprised that one who is so warm a friend can be so cool a lover.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: To be explicit, my dear Hastings, my chief inducement down was to be instrumental in forwarding your happiness, not my own. Miss Neville loves you, the family don’t know you; as my friend you are sure of a reception, and let honour do the rest.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: My dear Marlow! But I’ll suppress the emotion. Were I a wretch, meanly seeking to carry off a fortune, you should be the last man in the world I would apply to for assistance. But Miss Neville’s person is all I ask, and that is mine, both from her deceased father’s consent, and her own inclination.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Happy man! You have talents and art to captivate any woman. I’m doom’d to adore the sex, and yet to converse with the only part of it I despise. This stammer in my address, and this awkward prepossessing visage of mine, can never permit me to soar above the reach of a milliner’s ’prentice, or one of the duchesses of Drury-lane. Pshaw! this fellow here to interrupt us.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Gentlemen, once more you are heartily welcome. Which is Mr. Marlow? Sir, you are heartily welcome. It’s not my way, you see, to receive my friends with my back to the fire. I like give them a hearty reception in the old style at my gate. I like to see their horses and trunks taken care of.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: He has got our names from the servants already. We approve your caution and hospitality, sir. I have been thinking, George, of changing our travelling dresses in the morning. I am grown confoundedly ashamed of mine.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I beg, Mr. Marlow, you’ll use no ceremony in this house.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: I fancy, Charles, you’re right: the first blow is half the battle. I intend opening the campaign with the white and gold.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Mr. Marlow—Mr. Hastings—gentlemen—pray be under no constraint in this house. This is Liberty-hall, gentlemen. You may do just as you please here.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yet, George, if we open the campaign too fiercely at first, we may want ammunition before it is over. I think to reserve the embroidery to secure a retreat.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Your talking of a retreat, Mr. Marlow, puts me in mind of the Duke of Marlborough, when we went to besiege Denain. He first summoned the garrison——

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Don’t you think the ventre d’or waistcoat will do with the plain brown?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: He first summoned the garrison, which might consist of about five thousand men——

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: I think not: brown and yellow mix but very poorly.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I say, gentlemen, as I was telling you, be summoned the garrison, which might consist of about five thousand men——

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: The girls like finery.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Which might consist of about five thousand men, well appointed with stores, ammunition, and other implements of war. Now, says the Duke of Marlborough to George Brooks, that stood next to him—you must have heard of George Brooks—I’ll pawn my dukedom, says he, but I take that garrison without spilling a drop of blood. So——

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: What, my good friend, if you gave us a glass of punch in the mean time; it would help us to carry on the siege with vigour.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Punch, sir! This is the most unaccountable kind of modesty I ever met with.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yes, sir, punch. A glass of warm punch, after our journey, will be comfortable. This is Liberty-hall, you know.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Here’s a cup, sir.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: So this fellow, in his Liberty-hall, will only let us have just what he pleases.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I hope you’ll find it to your mind. I have prepared it with my own hands, and I believe you’ll own the ingredients are tolerable. Will you be so good as to pledge me, sir? Here, Mr. Marlow, here is to our better acquaintance.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: A very impudent fellow this! but he’s a character, and I’ll humour him a little. Sir, my service to you.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: I see this fellow wants to give us his company, and forgets that he’s an innkeeper, before he has learned to be a gentleman.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: From the excellence of your cup, my old friend, I suppose you have a good deal of business in this part of the country. Warm work, now and then, at elections, I suppose.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: No, sir, I have long given that work over. Since our betters have hit upon the expedient of electing each other, there is no business “for us that sell ale.”

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: So, then, you have no turn for politics, I find.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Not in the least. There was a time, indeed, I fretted myself about the mistakes of government, like other people; but finding myself every day grow more angry, and the government growing no better, I left it to mend itself. Since that, I no more trouble my head about Hyder Ally, or Ally Cawn, than about Ally Croker. Sir, my service to you.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: So that with eating above stairs, and drinking below, with receiving your friends within, and amusing them without, you lead a good pleasant bustling life of it.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I do stir about a great deal, that’s certain. Half the differences of the parish are adjusted in this very parlour.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: And you have an argument in your cup, old gentleman, better than any in Westminster-hall.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, young gentleman, that, and a little philosophy.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Well, this is the first time I ever heard of an innkeeper’s philosophy.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: So then, like an experienced general, you attack them on every quarter. If you find their reason manageable, you attack it with your philosophy; if you find they have no reason, you attack them with this. Here’s your health, my philosopher.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Good, very good, thank you; ha! ha! Your generalship puts me in mind of Prince Eugene, when he fought the Turks at the battle of Belgrade. You shall hear.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Instead of the battle of Belgrade, I believe it’s almost time to talk about supper. What has your philosophy got in the house for supper?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: For supper, sir! Was ever such a request to a man in his own house?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yes, sir, supper, sir; I begin to feel an appetite. I shall make devilish work to-night in the larder, I promise you.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Such a brazen dog sure never my eyes beheld. Why, really, sir, as for supper I can’t well tell. My Dorothy and the cook-maid settle these things between them. I leave these kind of things entirely to them.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: You do, do you?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Entirely. By the bye, I believe they are in actual consultation upon what’s for supper this moment in the kitchen.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Then I beg they’ll admit me as one of their privy council. It’s a way I have got. When I travel, I always chose to regulate my own supper. Let the cook be called. No offence I hope, sir.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: O no, sir, none in the least; yet I don’t know how; our Bridget, the cook-maid, is not very communicative upon these occasions. Should we send for her, she might scold us all out of the house.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Let’s see your list of the larder then. I ask it as a favour. I always match my appetite to my bill of fare.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Sir, he’s very right, and it’s my way too.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Sir, you have a right to command here. Here, Roger, bring us the bill of fare for to-night’s supper: I believe it’s drawn out—Your manner, Mr. Hastings, puts me in mind of my uncle, Colonel Wallop. It was a saying of his, that no man was sure of his supper till he had eaten it.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: All upon the high rope! His uncle a colonel! we shall soon hear of his mother being a justice of the peace. But let’s hear the bill of fare.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: What’s here? For the first course; for the second course; for the dessert. The devil, sir, do you think we have brought down a whole Joiners’ Company, or the corporation of Bedford, to eat up such a supper? Two or three little things, clean and comfortable, will do.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But let’s hear it.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: For the first course, at the top, a pig and prune sauce.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Damn your pig, I say.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: And damn your prune sauce, say I.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And yet, gentlemen, to men that are hungry, pig with prune sauce is very good eating.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: At the bottom, a calf’s tongue and brains.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Let your brains be knocked out, my good sir, I don’t like them.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Or you may clap them on a plate by themselves. I do.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Their impudence confounds me. Gentlemen, you are my guests, make what alterations you please. Is there anything else you wish to retrench or alter, gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Item, a pork pie, a boiled rabbit and sausages, a Florentine, a shaking pudding, and a dish of tiff—taff—taffety cream.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Confound your made dishes; I shall be as much at a loss in this house as at a green and yellow dinner at the French ambassador’s table. I’m for plain eating.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I’m sorry, gentlemen, that I have nothing you like, but if there be anything you have a particular fancy to——

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Why, really, sir, your bill of fare is so exquisite, that any one part of it is full as good as another. Send us what you please. So much for supper. And now to see that our beds are aired, and properly taken care of.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I entreat you’ll leave that to me. You shall not stir a step.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Leave that to you! I protest, sir, you must excuse me, I always look to these things myself.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I must insist, sir, you’ll make yourself easy on that head.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: You see I’m resolved on it. A very troublesome fellow this, as I ever met with.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, sir, I’m resolved at least to attend you. This may be modern modesty, but I never saw anything look so like old-fashioned impudence.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: So I find this fellow’s civilities begin to grow troublesome. But who can be angry at those assiduities which are meant to please him? Ha! what do I see? Miss Neville, by all that’s happy!

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: My dear Hastings! To what unexpected good fortune, to what accident, am I to ascribe this happy meeting?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Rather let me ask the same question, as I could never have hoped to meet my dearest Constance at an inn.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: An inn! sure you mistake: my aunt, my guardian, lives here. What could induce you to think this house an inn?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: My friend, Mr. Marlow, with whom I came down, and I, have been sent here as to an inn, I assure you. A young fellow, whom we accidentally met at a house hard by, directed us hither.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Certainly it must be one of my hopeful cousin’s tricks, of whom you have heard me talk so often; ha! ha! ha!

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: He whom your aunt intends for you? he of whom I have such just apprehensions?

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: You have nothing to fear from him, I assure you. You’d adore him, if you knew how heartily he despises me. My aunt knows it too, and has undertaken to court me for him, and actually begins to think she has made a conquest.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Thou dear dissembler! You must know, my Constance, I have just seized this happy opportunity of my friend’s visit here to get admittance into the family. The horses that carried us down are now fatigued with their journey, but they’ll soon be refreshed; and then, if my dearest girl will trust in her faithful Hastings, we shall soon be landed in France, where even among slaves the laws of marriage are respected.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I have often told you, that though ready to obey you, I yet should leave my little fortune behind with reluctance. The greatest part of it was left me by my uncle, the India director, and chiefly consists in jewels. I have been for some time persuading my aunt to let me wear them. I fancy I’m very near succeeding. The instant they are put into my possession, you shall find me ready to make them and myself yours.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Perish the baubles! Your person is all I desire. In the mean time, my friend Marlow must not be let into his mistake. I know the strange reserve of his temper is such, that if abruptly informed of it, he would instantly quit the house before our plan was ripe for execution.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: But how shall we keep him in the deception? Miss Hardcastle is just returned from walking; what if we still continue to deceive him?——This, this way——

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: The assiduities of these good people teaze me beyond bearing. My host seems to think it ill manners to leave me alone, and so he claps not only himself, but his old-fashioned wife, on my back. They talk of coming to sup with us too; and then, I suppose, we are to run the gantlet through all the rest of the family.—What have we got here?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: My dear Charles! Let me congratulate you!—The most fortunate accident!—Who do you think is just alighted?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Cannot guess.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Our mistresses, boy, Miss Hardcastle and Miss Neville. Give me leave to introduce Miss Constance Neville to your acquaintance. Happening to dine in the neighbourhood, they called on their return to take fresh horses here. Miss Hardcastle has just stept into the next room, and will be back in an instant. Wasn’t it lucky? eh!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I have been mortified enough of all conscience, and here comes something to complete my embarrassment.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Well, but wasn’t it the most fortunate thing in the world?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Oh! yes. Very fortunate—a most joyful encounter—But our dresses, George, you know are in disorder—What if we should postpone the happiness till to-morrow?—To-morrow at her own house—It will be every bit as convenient—and rather more respectful—To-morrow let it be.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: By no means, sir. Your ceremony will displease her. The disorder of your dress will show the ardour of your impatience. Besides, she knows you are in the house, and will permit you to see her.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: O! the devil! how shall I support it? Hem! hem! Hastings, you must not go. You are to assist me, you know. I shall be confoundedly ridiculous. Yet, hang it! I’ll take courage. Hem!

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Pshaw, man! it’s but the first plunge, and all’s over. She’s but a woman, you know.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: And, of all women, she that I dread most to encounter.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Miss Hardcastle, Mr. Marlow. I’m proud of bringing two persons of such merit together, that only want to know, to esteem each other.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Now for meeting my modest gentleman with a demure face, and quite in his own manner. I’m glad of your safe arrival, sir. I’m told you had some accidents by the way.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Only a few, madam. Yes, we had some. Yes, madam, a good many accidents, but should be sorry—madam—or rather glad of any accidents—that are so agreeably concluded. Hem!

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: You never spoke better in your whole life. Keep it up, and I’ll insure you the victory.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I’m afraid you flatter, sir. You that have seen so much of the finest company, can find little entertainment in an obscure corner of the country.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I have lived, indeed, in the world, madam; but I have kept very little company. I have been but an observer upon life, madam, while others were enjoying it.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: But that, I am told, is the way to enjoy it at last.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Cicero never spoke better. Once more, and you are confirmed in assurance for ever.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Hem! Stand by me, then, and when I’m down, throw in a word or two, to set me up again.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: An observer, like you, upon life were, I fear, disagreeably employed, since you must have had much more to censure than to approve.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Pardon me, madam. I was always willing to be amused. The folly of most people is rather an object of mirth than uneasiness.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Bravo, bravo. Never spoke so well in your whole life. Well, Miss Hardcastle, I see that you and Mr. Marlow are going to be very good company. I believe our being here will but embarrass the interview.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Not in the least, Mr. Hastings. We like your company of all things. Zounds! George, sure you won’t go? how can you leave us?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Our presence will but spoil conversation, so we’ll retire to the next room. You don’t consider, man, that we are to manage a little tete-a-tete of our own.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: But you have not been wholly an observer, I presume, sir: the ladies, I should hope, have employed some part of your addresses.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Pardon me, madam, I—I—I—as yet have studied—only—to—deserve them.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And that, some say, is the very worst way to obtain them.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Perhaps so, madam. But I love to converse only with the more grave and sensible part of the sex. But I’m afraid I grow tiresome.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Not at all, sir; there is nothing I like so much as grave conversation myself; I could hear it for ever. Indeed, I have often been surprised how a man of sentiment could ever admire those light airy pleasures, where nothing reaches the heart.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: It’s——a disease——of the mind, madam. In the variety of tastes there must be some who, wanting a relish——for——um—a—um.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I understand you, sir. There must be some, who, wanting a relish for refined pleasures, pretend to despise what they are incapable of tasting.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: My meaning, madam, but infinitely better expressed. And I can’t help observing——a——

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Who could ever suppose this fellow impudent upon some occasions? You were going to observe, sir——

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I was observing, madam—I protest, madam, I forget what I was going to observe.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I vow and so do I. You were observing, sir, that in this age of hypocrisy—something about hypocrisy, sir.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yes, madam. In this age of hypocrisy there are few who upon strict inquiry do not—a—a—a—

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I understand you perfectly, sir.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Egad! and that’s more than I do myself.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You mean that in this hypocritical age there are few that do not condemn in public what they practise in private, and think they pay every debt to virtue when they praise it.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: True, madam; those who have most virtue in their mouths, have least of it in their bosoms. But I’m sure I tire you, madam.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Not in the least, sir; there’s something so agreeable and spirited in your manner, such life and force—pray, sir, go on.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yes, madam. I was saying——that there are some occasions, when a total want of courage, madam, destroys all the——and puts us——upon a—a—a—

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I agree with you entirely; a want of courage upon some occasions assumes the appearance of ignorance, and betrays us when we most want to excel. I beg you’ll proceed.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yes, madam. Morally speaking, madam—But I see Miss Neville expecting us in the next room. I would not intrude for the world.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I protest, sir, I never was more agreeably entertained in all my life. Pray go on.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yes, madam, I was——But she beckons us to join her. Madam, shall I do myself the honour to attend you?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, then, I’ll follow.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: This pretty smooth dialogue has done for me.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ha! ha! ha! Was there ever such a sober, sentimental interview? I’m certain he scarce looked in my face the whole time. Yet the fellow, but for his unaccountable bashfulness, is pretty well too. He has good sense, but then so buried in his fears, that it fatigues one more than ignorance. If I could teach him a little confidence, it would be doing somebody that I know of a piece of service. But who is that somebody?—That, faith, is a question I can scarce answer.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: What do you follow me for, cousin Con? I wonder you’re not ashamed to be so very engaging.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I hope, cousin, one may speak to one’s own relations, and not be to blame.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ay, but I know what sort of a relation you want to make me, though; but it won’t do. I tell you, cousin Con, it won’t do; so I beg you’ll keep your distance, I want no nearer relationship.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well! I vow, Mr. Hastings, you are very entertaining. There’s nothing in the world I love to talk of so much as London, and the fashions, though I was never there myself.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Never there! You amaze me! From your air and manner, I concluded you had been bred all your life either at Ranelagh, St. James’s, or Tower Wharf.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: O! sir, you’re only pleased to say so. We country persons can have no manner at all. I’m in love with the town, and that serves to raise me above some of our neighbouring rustics; but who can have a manner, that has never seen the Pantheon, the Grotto Gardens, the Borough, and such places where the nobility chiefly resort? All I can do is to enjoy London at second-hand. I take care to know every tete-a-tete from the Scandalous Magazine, and have all the fashions, as they come out, in a letter from the two Miss Rickets of Crooked Lane. Pray how do you like this head, Mr. Hastings?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Extremely elegant and degagee, upon my word, madam. Your friseur is a Frenchman, I suppose?

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I protest, I dressed it myself from a print in the Ladies’ Memorandum-book for the last year.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Indeed! Such a head in a side-box at the play-house would draw as many gazers as my Lady Mayoress at a City Ball.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I vow, since inoculation began, there is no such thing to be seen as a plain woman; so one must dress a little particular, or one may escape in the crowd.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But that can never be your case, madam, in any dress.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Yet, what signifies my dressing when I have such a piece of antiquity by my side as Mr. Hardcastle: all I can say will never argue down a single button from his clothes. I have often wanted him to throw off his great flaxen wig, and where he was bald, to plaster it over, like my Lord Pately, with powder.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: You are right, madam; for, as among the ladies there are none ugly, so among the men there are none old.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: But what do you think his answer was? Why, with his usual Gothic vivacity, he said I only wanted him to throw off his wig, to convert it into a tete for my own wearing.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Intolerable! At your age you may wear what you please, and it must become you.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Pray, Mr. Hastings, what do you take to be the most fashionable age about town?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Some time ago, forty was all the mode; but I’m told the ladies intend to bring up fifty for the ensuing winter.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Seriously. Then I shall be too young for the fashion.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: No lady begins now to put on jewels till she’s past forty. For instance, Miss there, in a polite circle, would be considered as a child, as a mere maker of samplers.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And yet Mrs. Niece thinks herself as much a woman, and is as fond of jewels, as the oldest of us all.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Your niece, is she? And that young gentleman, a brother of yours, I should presume?

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: My son, sir. They are contracted to each other. Observe their little sports. They fall in and out ten times a day, as if they were man and wife already. Well, Tony, child, what soft things are you saying to your cousin Constance this evening?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I have been saying no soft things; but that it’s very hard to be followed about so. Ecod! I’ve not a place in the house now that’s left to myself, but the stable.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Never mind him, Con, my dear. He’s in another story behind your back.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: There’s something generous in my cousin’s manner. He falls out before faces to be forgiven in private.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: That’s a damned confounded—crack.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ah! he’s a sly one. Don’t you think they are like each other about the mouth, Mr. Hastings? The Blenkinsop mouth to a T. They’re of a size too. Back to back, my pretties, that Mr. Hastings may see you. Come, Tony.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: You had as good not make me, I tell you.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: O lud! he has almost cracked my head.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: O, the monster! For shame, Tony. You a man, and behave so!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: If I’m a man, let me have my fortin. Ecod! I’ll not be made a fool of no longer.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Is this, ungrateful boy, all that I’m to get for the pains I have taken in your education? I that have rocked you in your cradle, and fed that pretty mouth with a spoon! Did not I work that waistcoat to make you genteel? Did not I prescribe for you every day, and weep while the receipt was operating?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ecod! you had reason to weep, for you have been dosing me ever since I was born. I have gone through every receipt in the Complete Huswife ten times over; and you have thoughts of coursing me through Quincy next spring. But, ecod! I tell you, I’ll not be made a fool of no longer.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Wasn’t it all for your good, viper? Wasn’t it all for your good?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I wish you’d let me and my good alone, then. Snubbing this way when I’m in spirits. If I’m to have any good, let it come of itself; not to keep dinging it, dinging it into one so.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: That’s false; I never see you when you’re in spirits. No, Tony, you then go to the alehouse or kennel. I’m never to be delighted with your agreeable wild notes, unfeeling monster!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ecod! mamma, your own notes are the wildest of the two.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Was ever the like? But I see he wants to break my heart, I see he does.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Dear madam, permit me to lecture the young gentleman a little. I’m certain I can persuade him to his duty.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, I must retire. Come, Constance, my love. You see, Mr. Hastings, the wretchedness of my situation: was ever poor woman so plagued with a dear sweet, pretty, provoking, undutiful boy?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: “There was a young man riding by, and fain would have his will. Rang do didlo dee.”——Don’t mind her. Let her cry. It’s the comfort of her heart. I have seen her and sister cry over a book for an hour together; and they said they liked the book the better the more it made them cry.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Then you’re no friend to the ladies, I find, my pretty young gentleman?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: That’s as I find ’um.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Not to her of your mother’s choosing, I dare answer? And yet she appears to me a pretty well-tempered girl.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: That’s because you don’t know her as well as I. Ecod! I know every inch about her; and there’s not a more bitter cantankerous toad in all Christendom.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Pretty encouragement this for a lover!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I have seen her since the height of that. She has as many tricks as a hare in a thicket, or a colt the first day’s breaking.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: To me she appears sensible and silent.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ay, before company. But when she’s with her playmate, she’s as loud as a hog in a gate.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But there is a meek modesty about her that charms me.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Yes, but curb her never so little, she kicks up, and you’re flung in a ditch.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Well, but you must allow her a little beauty.—Yes, you must allow her some beauty.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Bandbox! She’s all a made-up thing, mun. Ah! could you but see Bet Bouncer of these parts, you might then talk of beauty. Ecod, she has two eyes as black as sloes, and cheeks as broad and red as a pulpit cushion. She’d make two of she.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Well, what say you to a friend that would take this bitter bargain off your hands?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Anon.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Would you thank him that would take Miss Neville, and leave you to happiness and your dear Betsy?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ay; but where is there such a friend, for who would take her?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: I am he. If you but assist me, I’ll engage to whip her off to France, and you shall never hear more of her.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Assist you! Ecod I will, to the last drop of my blood. I’ll clap a pair of horses to your chaise that shall trundle you off in a twinkling, and may he get you a part of her fortin beside, in jewels, that you little dream of.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: My dear ’squire, this looks like a lad of spirit.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Come along, then, and you shall see more of my spirit before you have done with me. “We are the boys That fears no noise Where the thundering cannons roar.”

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: What could my old friend Sir Charles mean by recommending his son as the modestest young man in town? To me he appears the most impudent piece of brass that ever spoke with a tongue. He has taken possession of the easy chair by the fire-side already. He took off his boots in the parlour, and desired me to see them taken care of. I’m desirous to know how his impudence affects my daughter. She will certainly be shocked at it.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, my Kate, I see you have changed your dress, as I bade you; and yet, I believe, there was no great occasion.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I find such a pleasure, sir, in obeying your commands, that I take care to observe them without ever debating their propriety.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And yet, Kate, I sometimes give you some cause, particularly when I recommended my modest gentleman to you as a lover to-day.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You taught me to expect something extraordinary, and I find the original exceeds the description.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I was never so surprised in my life! He has quite confounded all my faculties!

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I never saw anything like it: and a man of the world too!

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, he learned it all abroad—what a fool was I, to think a young man could learn modesty by travelling. He might as soon learn wit at a masquerade.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: It seems all natural to him.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: A good deal assisted by bad company and a French dancing-master.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Sure you mistake, papa! A French dancing-master could never have taught him that timid look—that awkward address—that bashful manner—

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Whose look? whose manner, child?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Mr. Marlow’s: his mauvaise honte, his timidity, struck me at the first sight.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Then your first sight deceived you; for I think him one of the most brazen first sights that ever astonished my senses.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Sure, sir, you rally! I never saw any one so modest.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And can you be serious? I never saw such a bouncing, swaggering puppy since I was born. Bully Dawson was but a fool to him.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Surprising! He met me with a respectful bow, a stammering voice, and a look fixed on the ground.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: He met me with a loud voice, a lordly air, and a familiarity that made my blood freeze again.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: He treated me with diffidence and respect; censured the manners of the age; admired the prudence of girls that never laughed; tired me with apologies for being tiresome; then left the room with a bow, and “Madam, I would not for the world detain you.”

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: He spoke to me as if he knew me all his life before; asked twenty questions, and never waited for an answer; interrupted my best remarks with some silly pun; and when I was in my best story of the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene, he asked if I had not a good hand at making punch. Yes, Kate, he asked your father if he was a maker of punch!

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: One of us must certainly be mistaken.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: If he be what he has shown himself, I’m determined he shall never have my consent.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And if he be the sullen thing I take him, he shall never have mine.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: In one thing then we are agreed—to reject him.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Yes: but upon conditions. For if you should find him less impudent, and I more presuming—if you find him more respectful, and I more importunate—I don’t know—the fellow is well enough for a man—Certainly, we don’t meet many such at a horse-race in the country.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: If we should find him so——But that’s impossible. The first appearance has done my business. I’m seldom deceived in that.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And yet there may be many good qualities under that first appearance.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, when a girl finds a fellow’s outside to her taste, she then sets about guessing the rest of his furniture. With her, a smooth face stands for good sense, and a genteel figure for every virtue.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I hope, sir, a conversation begun with a compliment to my good sense, won’t end with a sneer at my understanding?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Pardon me, Kate. But if young Mr. Brazen can find the art of reconciling contradictions, he may please us both, perhaps.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And as one of us must be mistaken, what if we go to make further discoveries?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Agreed. But depend on’t I’m in the right.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And depend on’t I’m not much in the wrong.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ecod! I have got them. Here they are. My cousin Con’s necklaces, bobs and all. My mother shan’t cheat the poor souls out of their fortin neither. O! my genus, is that you?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: My dear friend, how have you managed with your mother? I hope you have amused her with pretending love for your cousin, and that you are willing to be reconciled at last? Our horses will be refreshed in a short time, and we shall soon be ready to set off.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: And here’s something to bear your charges by the way; your sweetheart’s jewels. Keep them: and hang those, I say, that would rob you of one of them.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But how have you procured them from your mother?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ask me no questions, and I’ll tell you no fibs. I procured them by the rule of thumb. If I had not a key to every drawer in mother’s bureau, how could I go to the alehouse so often as I do? An honest man may rob himself of his own at any time.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Thousands do it every day. But to be plain with you; Miss Neville is endeavouring to procure them from her aunt this very instant. If she succeeds, it will be the most delicate way at least of obtaining them.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Well, keep them, till you know how it will be. But I know how it will be well enough; she’d as soon part with the only sound tooth in her head.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But I dread the effects of her resentment, when she finds she has lost them.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Never you mind her resentment, leave ME to manage that. I don’t value her resentment the bounce of a cracker. Zounds! here they are. Morrice! Prance!

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Indeed, Constance, you amaze me. Such a girl as you want jewels! It will be time enough for jewels, my dear, twenty years hence, when your beauty begins to want repairs.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: But what will repair beauty at forty, will certainly improve it at twenty, madam.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Yours, my dear, can admit of none. That natural blush is beyond a thousand ornaments. Besides, child, jewels are quite out at present. Don’t you see half the ladies of our acquaintance, my Lady Kill-daylight, and Mrs. Crump, and the rest of them, carry their jewels to town, and bring nothing but paste and marcasites back.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: But who knows, madam, but somebody that shall be nameless would like me best with all my little finery about me?

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Consult your glass, my dear, and then see if, with such a pair of eyes, you want any better sparklers. What do you think, Tony, my dear? does your cousin Con. want any jewels in your eyes to set off her beauty?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: That’s as thereafter may be.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: My dear aunt, if you knew how it would oblige me.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: A parcel of old-fashioned rose and table-cut things. They would make you look like the court of King Solomon at a puppet-show. Besides, I believe, I can’t readily come at them. They may be missing, for aught I know to the contrary.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Then why don’t you tell her so at once, as she’s so longing for them? Tell her they’re lost. It’s the only way to quiet her. Say they’re lost, and call me to bear witness.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You know, my dear, I’m only keeping them for you. So if I say they’re gone, you’ll bear me witness, will you? He! he! he!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Never fear me. Ecod! I’ll say I saw them taken out with my own eyes.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I desire them but for a day, madam. Just to be permitted to show them as relics, and then they may be locked up again.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: To be plain with you, my dear Constance, if I could find them you should have them. They’re missing, I assure you. Lost, for aught I know; but we must have patience wherever they are.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I’ll not believe it! this is but a shallow pretence to deny me. I know they are too valuable to be so slightly kept, and as you are to answer for the loss—

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Don’t be alarmed, Constance. If they be lost, I must restore an equivalent. But my son knows they are missing, and not to be found.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: That I can bear witness to. They are missing, and not to be found; I’ll take my oath on’t.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You must learn resignation, my dear; for though we lose our fortune, yet we should not lose our patience. See me, how calm I am.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Ay, people are generally calm at the misfortunes of others.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Now I wonder a girl of your good sense should waste a thought upon such trumpery. We shall soon find them; and in the mean time you shall make use of my garnets till your jewels be found.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I detest garnets.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: The most becoming things in the world to set off a clear complexion. You have often seen how well they look upon me. You SHALL have them.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I dislike them of all things. You shan’t stir.—Was ever anything so provoking, to mislay my own jewels, and force me to wear her trumpery?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Don’t be a fool. If she gives you the garnets, take what you can get. The jewels are your own already. I have stolen them out of her bureau, and she does not know it. Fly to your spark, he’ll tell you more of the matter. Leave me to manage her.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: My dear cousin!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Vanish. She’s here, and has missed them already. Zounds! how she fidgets and spits about like a Catherine wheel.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Confusion! thieves! robbers! we are cheated, plundered, broke open, undone.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: What’s the matter, what’s the matter, mamma? I hope nothing has happened to any of the good family!

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: We are robbed. My bureau has been broken open, the jewels taken out, and I’m undone.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Oh! is that all? Ha! ha! ha! By the laws, I never saw it acted better in my life. Ecod, I thought you was ruined in earnest, ha! ha! ha!

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Why, boy, I AM ruined in earnest. My bureau has been broken open, and all taken away.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Stick to that: ha! ha! ha! stick to that. I’ll bear witness, you know; call me to bear witness.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I tell you, Tony, by all that’s precious, the jewels are gone, and I shall be ruined for ever.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Sure I know they’re gone, and I’m to say so.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: My dearest Tony, but hear me. They’re gone, I say.

speeches.speaker: TONY
