speeches.text: By the laws, mamma, you make me for to laugh, ha! ha! I know who took them well enough, ha! ha! ha!

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Was there ever such a blockhead, that can’t tell the difference between jest and earnest? I tell you I’m not in jest, booby.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: That’s right, that’s right; you must be in a bitter passion, and then nobody will suspect either of us. I’ll bear witness that they are gone.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Was there ever such a cross-grained brute, that won’t hear me? Can you bear witness that you’re no better than a fool? Was ever poor woman so beset with fools on one hand, and thieves on the other?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I can bear witness to that.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Bear witness again, you blockhead you, and I’ll turn you out of the room directly. My poor niece, what will become of her? Do you laugh, you unfeeling brute, as if you enjoyed my distress?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I can bear witness to that.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Do you insult me, monster? I’ll teach you to vex your mother, I will.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I can bear witness to that.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: What an unaccountable creature is that brother of mine, to send them to the house as an inn! ha! ha! I don’t wonder at his impudence.

speeches.speaker: MAID
speeches.text: But what is more, madam, the young gentleman, as you passed by in your present dress, asked me if you were the bar-maid. He mistook you for the bar-maid, madam.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Did he? Then as I live, I’m resolved to keep up the delusion. Tell me, Pimple, how do you like my present dress? Don’t you think I look something like Cherry in the Beaux Stratagem?

speeches.speaker: MAID
speeches.text: It’s the dress, madam, that every lady wears in the country, but when she visits or receives company.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And are you sure he does not remember my face or person?

speeches.speaker: MAID
speeches.text: Certain of it.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I vow, I thought so; for, though we spoke for some time together, yet his fears were such, that he never once looked up during the interview. Indeed, if he had, my bonnet would have kept him from seeing me.

speeches.speaker: MAID
speeches.text: But what do you hope from keeping him in his mistake?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: In the first place I shall be seen, and that is no small advantage to a girl who brings her face to market. Then I shall perhaps make an acquaintance, and that’s no small victory gained over one who never addresses any but the wildest of her sex. But my chief aim is, to take my gentleman off his guard, and, like an invisible champion of romance, examine the giant’s force before I offer to combat.

speeches.speaker: MAID
speeches.text: But you are sure you can act your part, and disguise your voice so that he may mistake that, as he has already mistaken your person?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Never fear me. I think I have got the true bar cant—Did your honour call?—Attend the Lion there—Pipes and tobacco for the Angel.—The Lamb has been outrageous this half-hour.

speeches.speaker: MAID
speeches.text: It will do, madam. But he’s here.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: What a bawling in every part of the house! I have scarce a moment’s repose. If I go to the best room, there I find my host and his story: if I fly to the gallery, there we have my hostess with her curtsey down to the ground. I have at last got a moment to myself, and now for recollection.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Did you call, sir? Did your honour call?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: As for Miss Hardcastle, she’s too grave and sentimental for me.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Did your honour call?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: No, child. Besides, from the glimpse I had of her, I think she squints.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I’m sure, sir, I heard the bell ring.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: No, no. I have pleased my father, however, by coming down, and I’ll to-morrow please myself by returning.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Perhaps the other gentleman called, sir?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I tell you, no.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I should be glad to know, sir. We have such a parcel of servants!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: No, no, I tell you. Yes, child, I think I did call. I wanted—I wanted—I vow, child, you are vastly handsome.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: O la, sir, you’ll make one ashamed.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Never saw a more sprightly malicious eye. Yes, yes, my dear, I did call. Have you got any of your—a—what d’ye call it in the house?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: No, sir, we have been out of that these ten days.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: One may call in this house, I find, to very little purpose. Suppose I should call for a taste, just by way of a trial, of the nectar of your lips; perhaps I might be disappointed in that too.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Nectar! nectar! That’s a liquor there’s no call for in these parts. French, I suppose. We sell no French wines here, sir.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Of true English growth, I assure you.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Then it’s odd I should not know it. We brew all sorts of wines in this house, and I have lived here these eighteen years.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Eighteen years! Why, one would think, child, you kept the bar before you were born. How old are you?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: O! sir, I must not tell my age. They say women and music should never be dated.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: To guess at this distance, you can’t be much above forty. Yet, nearer, I don’t think so much. By coming close to some women they look younger still; but when we come very close indeed—.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Pray, sir, keep your distance. One would think you wanted to know one’s age, as they do horses, by mark of mouth.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I protest, child, you use me extremely ill. If you keep me at this distance, how is it possible you and I can ever be acquainted?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And who wants to be acquainted with you? I want no such acquaintance, not I. I’m sure you did not treat Miss Hardcastle, that was here awhile ago, in this obstropalous manner. I’ll warrant me, before her you looked dashed, and kept bowing to the ground, and talked, for all the world, as if you was before a justice of peace.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Egad, she has hit it, sure enough! In awe of her, child? Ha! ha! ha! A mere awkward squinting thing; no, no. I find you don’t know me. I laughed and rallied her a little; but I was unwilling to be too severe. No, I could not be too severe, curse me!

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: O! then, sir, you are a favourite, I find, among the ladies?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yes, my dear, a great favourite. And yet hang me, I don’t see what they find in me to follow. At the Ladies’ Club in town I’m called their agreeable Rattle. Rattle, child, is not my real name, but one I’m known by. My name is Solomons; Mr. Solomons, my dear, at your service.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Hold, sir; you are introducing me to your club, not to yourself. And you’re so great a favourite there, you say?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yes, my dear. There’s Mrs. Mantrap, Lady Betty Blackleg, the Countess of Sligo, Mrs. Langhorns, old Miss Biddy Buckskin, and your humble servant, keep up the spirit of the place.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Then it’s a very merry place, I suppose?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yes, as merry as cards, supper, wine, and old women can make us.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And their agreeable Rattle, ha! ha! ha!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Egad! I don’t quite like this chit. She looks knowing, methinks. You laugh, child?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I can’t but laugh, to think what time they all have for minding their work or their family.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: All’s well; she don’t laugh at me. Do you ever work, child?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, sure. There’s not a screen or quilt in the whole house but what can bear witness to that.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Odso! then you must show me your embroidery. I embroider and draw patterns myself a little. If you want a judge of your work, you must apply to me.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, but the colours do not look well by candlelight. You shall see all in the morning.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: And why not now, my angel? Such beauty fires beyond the power of resistance.—Pshaw! the father here! My old luck: I never nicked seven that I did not throw ames ace three times following.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: So, madam. So, I find THIS is your MODEST lover. This is your humble admirer, that kept his eyes fixed on the ground, and only adored at humble distance. Kate, Kate, art thou not ashamed to deceive your father so?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Never trust me, dear papa, but he’s still the modest man I first took him for; you’ll be convinced of it as well as I.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: By the hand of my body, I believe his impudence is infectious! Didn’t I see him seize your hand? Didn’t I see him haul you about like a milkmaid? And now you talk of his respect and his modesty, forsooth!

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: But if I shortly convince you of his modesty, that he has only the faults that will pass off with time, and the virtues that will improve with age, I hope you’ll forgive him.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: The girl would actually make one run mad! I tell you, I’ll not be convinced. I am convinced. He has scarce been three hours in the house, and he has already encroached on all my prerogatives. You may like his impudence, and call it modesty; but my son-in-law, madam, must have very different qualifications.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Sir, I ask but this night to convince you.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You shall not have half the time, for I have thoughts of turning him out this very hour.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Give me that hour then, and I hope to satisfy you.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, an hour let it be then. But I’ll have no trifling with your father. All fair and open, do you mind me.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I hope, sir, you have ever found that I considered your commands as my pride; for your kindness is such, that my duty as yet has been inclination.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: You surprise me; Sir Charles Marlow expected here this night! Where have you had your information?

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: You may depend upon it. I just saw his letter to Mr. Hardcastle, in which he tells him he intends setting out a few hours after his son.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Then, my Constance, all must be completed before he arrives. He knows me; and should he find me here, would discover my name, and perhaps my designs, to the rest of the family.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: The jewels, I hope, are safe?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Yes, yes, I have sent them to Marlow, who keeps the keys of our baggage. In the mean time, I’ll go to prepare matters for our elopement. I have had the ’squire’s promise of a fresh pair of horses; and if I should not see him again, will write him further directions.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Well! success attend you. In the mean time I’ll go and amuse my aunt with the old pretence of a violent passion for my cousin.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I wonder what Hastings could mean by sending me so valuable a thing as a casket to keep for him, when he knows the only place I have is the seat of a post-coach at an inn-door. Have you deposited the casket with the landlady, as I ordered you? Have you put it into her own hands?

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
speeches.text: Yes, your honour.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: She said she’d keep it safe, did she?

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
speeches.text: Yes, she said she’d keep it safe enough; she asked me how I came by it; and she said she had a great mind to make me give an account of myself.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Ha! ha! ha! They’re safe, however. What an unaccountable set of beings have we got amongst! This little bar-maid though runs in my head most strangely, and drives out the absurdities of all the rest of the family. She’s mine, she must be mine, or I’m greatly mistaken.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Bless me! I quite forgot to tell her that I intended to prepare at the bottom of the garden. Marlow here, and in spirits too!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Give me joy, George! Crown me, shadow me with laurels! Well, George, after all, we modest fellows don’t want for success among the women.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Some women, you mean. But what success has your honour’s modesty been crowned with now, that it grows so insolent upon us?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Didn’t you see the tempting, brisk, lovely little thing, that runs about the house with a bunch of keys to its girdle?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Well, and what then?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: She’s mine, you rogue you. Such fire, such motion, such eyes, such lips; but, egad! she would not let me kiss them though.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But are you so sure, so very sure of her?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Why, man, she talked of showing me her work above stairs, and I am to improve the pattern.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But how can you, Charles, go about to rob a woman of her honour?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Pshaw! pshaw! We all know the honour of the bar-maid of an inn. I don’t intend to rob her, take my word for it; there’s nothing in this house I shan’t honestly pay for.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: I believe the girl has virtue.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: And if she has, I should be the last man in the world that would attempt to corrupt it.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: You have taken care, I hope, of the casket I sent you to lock up? Is it in safety?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Yes, yes. It’s safe enough. I have taken care of it. But how could you think the seat of a post-coach at an inn-door a place of safety? Ah! numskull! I have taken better precautions for you than you did for yourself——I have——

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: What?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I have sent it to the landlady to keep for you.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: To the landlady!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: The landlady.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: You did?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I did. She’s to be answerable for its forthcoming, you know.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Yes, she’ll bring it forth with a witness.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Wasn’t I right? I believe you’ll allow that I acted prudently upon this occasion.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: He must not see my uneasiness.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: You seem a little disconcerted though, methinks. Sure nothing has happened?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: No, nothing. Never was in better spirits in all my life. And so you left it with the landlady, who, no doubt, very readily undertook the charge.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Rather too readily. For she not only kept the casket, but, through her great precaution, was going to keep the messenger too. Ha! ha! ha!

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: He! he! he! They’re safe, however.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: As a guinea in a miser’s purse.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: So now all hopes of fortune are at an end, and we must set off without it. Well, Charles, I’ll leave you to your meditations on the pretty bar-maid, and, he! he! he! may you be as successful for yourself, as you have been for me!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Thank ye, George: I ask no more. Ha! ha! ha!

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I no longer know my own house. It’s turned all topsy-turvy. His servants have got drunk already. I’ll bear it no longer; and yet, from my respect for his father, I’ll be calm. Mr. Marlow, your servant. I’m your very humble servant.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Sir, your humble servant. What’s to be the wonder now?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I believe, sir, you must be sensible, sir, that no man alive ought to be more welcome than your father’s son, sir. I hope you think so?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I do from my soul, sir. I don’t want much entreaty. I generally make my father’s son welcome wherever he goes.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I believe you do, from my soul, sir. But though I say nothing to your own conduct, that of your servants is insufferable. Their manner of drinking is setting a very bad example in this house, I assure you.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I protest, my very good sir, that is no fault of mine. If they don’t drink as they ought, they are to blame. I ordered them not to spare the cellar. I did, I assure you. Here, let one of my servants come up. My positive directions were, that as I did not drink myself, they should make up for my deficiencies below.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Then they had your orders for what they do? I’m satisfied!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: They had, I assure you. You shall hear from one of themselves.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: You, Jeremy! Come forward, sirrah! What were my orders? Were you not told to drink freely, and call for what you thought fit, for the good of the house?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I begin to lose my patience.

speeches.speaker: JEREMY
speeches.text: Please your honour, liberty and Fleet-street for ever! Though I’m but a servant, I’m as good as another man. I’ll drink for no man before supper, sir, damme! Good liquor will sit upon a good supper, but a good supper will not sit upon——hiccup——on my conscience, sir.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: You see, my old friend, the fellow is as drunk as he can possibly be. I don’t know what you’d have more, unless you’d have the poor devil soused in a beer-barrel.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Zounds! he’ll drive me distracted, if I contain myself any longer. Mr. Marlow—Sir; I have submitted to your insolence for more than four hours, and I see no likelihood of its coming to an end. I’m now resolved to be master here, sir; and I desire that you and your drunken pack may leave my house directly.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Leave your house!——Sure you jest, my good friend! What? when I’m doing what I can to please you.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I tell you, sir, you don’t please me; so I desire you’ll leave my house.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Sure you cannot be serious? At this time o’ night, and such a night? You only mean to banter me.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I tell you, sir, I’m serious! and now that my passions are roused, I say this house is mine, sir; this house is mine, and I command you to leave it directly.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Ha! ha! ha! A puddle in a storm. I shan’t stir a step, I assure you. This your house, fellow! It’s my house. This is my house. Mine, while I choose to stay. What right have you to bid me leave this house, sir? I never met with such impudence, curse me; never in my whole life before.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Nor I, confound me if ever I did. To come to my house, to call for what he likes, to turn me out of my own chair, to insult the family, to order his servants to get drunk, and then to tell me, “This house is mine, sir.” By all that’s impudent, it makes me laugh. Ha! ha! ha! Pray, sir, as you take the house, what think you of taking the rest of the furniture? There’s a pair of silver candlesticks, and there’s a fire-screen, and here’s a pair of brazen-nosed bellows; perhaps you may take a fancy to them?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Bring me your bill, sir; bring me your bill, and let’s make no more words about it.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: There are a set of prints, too. What think you of the Rake’s Progress, for your own apartment?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Bring me your bill, I say; and I’ll leave you and your infernal house directly.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Then there’s a mahogany table that you may see your own face in.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: My bill, I say.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I had forgot the great chair for your own particular slumbers, after a hearty meal.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Zounds! bring me my bill, I say, and let’s hear no more on’t.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Young man, young man, from your father’s letter to me, I was taught to expect a well-bred modest man as a visitor here, but now I find him no better than a coxcomb and a bully; but he will be down here presently, and shall hear more of it.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: How’s this? Sure I have not mistaken the house. Everything looks like an inn. The servants cry, coming; the attendance is awkward; the bar-maid, too, to attend us. But she’s here, and will further inform me. Whither so fast, child? A word with you.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Let it be short, then. I’m in a hurry. I believe he begins to find out his mistake. But it’s too soon quite to undeceive him.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Pray, child, answer me one question. What are you, and what may your business in this house be?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: A relation of the family, sir.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: What, a poor relation.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Yes, sir. A poor relation, appointed to keep the keys, and to see that the guests want nothing in my power to give them.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: That is, you act as the bar-maid of this inn.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Inn! O law——what brought that in your head? One of the best families in the country keep an inn—Ha! ha! ha! old Mr. Hardcastle’s house an inn!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Mr. Hardcastle’s house! Is this Mr. Hardcastle’s house, child?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, sure! Whose else should it be?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: So then, all’s out, and I have been damnably imposed on. O, confound my stupid head, I shall be laughed at over the whole town. I shall be stuck up in caricatura in all the print-shops. The DULLISSIMO MACCARONI. To mistake this house of all others for an inn, and my father’s old friend for an innkeeper! What a swaggering puppy must he take me for! What a silly puppy do I find myself! There again, may I be hanged, my dear, but I mistook you for the bar-maid.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Dear me! dear me! I’m sure there’s nothing in my BEHAVIOUR to put me on a level with one of that stamp.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Nothing, my dear, nothing. But I was in for a list of blunders, and could not help making you a subscriber. My stupidity saw everything the wrong way. I mistook your assiduity for assurance, and your simplicity for allurement. But it’s over. This house I no more show MY face in.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I hope, sir, I have done nothing to disoblige you. I’m sure I should be sorry to affront any gentleman who has been so polite, and said so many civil things to me. I’m sure I should be sorry if he left the family upon my account. I’m sure I should be sorry if people said anything amiss, since I have no fortune but my character.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: By Heaven! she weeps. This is the first mark of tenderness I ever had from a modest woman, and it touches me. Excuse me, my lovely girl; you are the only part of the family I leave with reluctance. But to be plain with you, the difference of our birth, fortune, and education, makes an honourable connexion impossible; and I can never harbour a thought of seducing simplicity that trusted in my honour, of bringing ruin upon one whose only fault was being too lovely.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Generous man! I now begin to admire him. But I am sure my family is as good as Miss Hardcastle’s; and though I’m poor, that’s no great misfortune to a contented mind; and, until this moment, I never thought that it was bad to want fortune.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: And why now, my pretty simplicity?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Because it puts me at a distance from one that, if I had a thousand pounds, I would give it all to.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: This simplicity bewitches me, so that if I stay, I’m undone. I must make one bold effort, and leave her. Your partiality in my favour, my dear, touches me most sensibly: and were I to live for myself alone, I could easily fix my choice. But I owe too much to the opinion of the world, too much to the authority of a father; so that—I can scarcely speak it—it affects me. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I never knew half his merit till now. He shall not go, if I have power or art to detain him. I’ll still preserve the character in which I STOOPED TO CONQUER; but will undeceive my papa, who perhaps may laugh him out of his resolution.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ay, you may steal for yourselves the next time. I have done my duty. She has got the jewels again, that’s a sure thing; but she believes it was all a mistake of the servants.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: But, my dear cousin, sure you won’t forsake us in this distress? If she in the least suspects that I am going off, I shall certainly be locked up, or sent to my aunt Pedigree’s, which is ten times worse.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: To be sure, aunts of all kinds are damned bad things. But what can I do? I have got you a pair of horses that will fly like Whistle-jacket; and I’m sure you can’t say but I have courted you nicely before her face. Here she comes, we must court a bit or two more, for fear she should suspect us.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, I was greatly fluttered, to be sure. But my son tells me it was all a mistake of the servants. I shan’t be easy, however, till they are fairly married, and then let her keep her own fortune. But what do I see? fondling together, as I’m alive. I never saw Tony so sprightly before. Ah! have I caught you, my pretty doves? What, billing, exchanging stolen glances and broken murmurs? Ah!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: As for murmurs, mother, we grumble a little now and then, to be sure. But there’s no love lost between us.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: A mere sprinkling, Tony, upon the flame, only to make it burn brighter.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Cousin Tony promises to give us more of his company at home. Indeed, he shan’t leave us any more. It won’t leave us, cousin Tony, will it?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: O! it’s a pretty creature. No, I’d sooner leave my horse in a pound, than leave you when you smile upon one so. Your laugh makes you so becoming.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Agreeable cousin! Who can help admiring that natural humour, that pleasant, broad, red, thoughtless —ah! it’s a bold face.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Pretty innocence!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I’m sure I always loved cousin Con.’s hazle eyes, and her pretty long fingers, that she twists this way and that over the haspicholls, like a parcel of bobbins.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ah! he would charm the bird from the tree. I was never so happy before. My boy takes after his father, poor Mr. Lumpkin, exactly. The jewels, my dear Con., shall be yours incontinently. You shall have them. Isn’t he a sweet boy, my dear? You shall be married to-morrow, and we’ll put off the rest of his education, like Dr. Drowsy’s sermons, to a fitter opportunity.

speeches.speaker: DIGGORY
speeches.text: Where’s the ’squire? I have got a letter for your worship.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Give it to my mamma. She reads all my letters first.

speeches.speaker: DIGGORY
speeches.text: I had orders to deliver it into your own hands.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Who does it come from?

speeches.speaker: DIGGORY
speeches.text: Your worship mun ask that o’ the letter itself.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: I could wish to know though.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Undone! undone! A letter to him from Hastings. I know the hand. If my aunt sees it, we are ruined for ever. I’ll keep her employed a little if I can. But I have not told you, madam, of my cousin’s smart answer just now to Mr. Marlow. We so laughed.—You must know, madam.—This way a little, for he must not hear us.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: A damned cramp piece of penmanship, as ever I saw in my life. I can read your print hand very well. But here are such handles, and shanks, and dashes, that one can scarce tell the head from the tail.—“To Anthony Lumpkin, Esquire.” It’s very odd, I can read the outside of my letters, where my own name is, well enough; but when I come to open it, it’s all——buzz. That’s hard, very hard; for the inside of the letter is always the cream of the correspondence.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ha! ha! ha! Very well, very well. And so my son was too hard for the philosopher.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Yes, madam; but you must hear the rest, madam. A little more this way, or he may hear us. You’ll hear how he puzzled him again.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: He seems strangely puzzled now himself, methinks.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: A damned up and down hand, as if it was disguised in liquor.— Dear Sir,—ay, that’s that. Then there’s an M, and a T, and an S, but whether the next be an izzard, or an R, confound me, I cannot tell.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: What’s that, my dear? Can I give you any assistance?

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Pray, aunt, let me read it. Nobody reads a cramp hand better than I. Do you know who it is from?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Can’t tell, except from Dick Ginger, the feeder.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Ay, so it is. Dear ’Squire, hoping that you’re in health, as I am at this present. The gentlemen of the Shake-bag club has cut the gentlemen of Goose-green quite out of feather. The odds—um—odd battle—um—long fighting—um—here, here, it’s all about cocks and fighting; it’s of no consequence; here, put it up, put it up.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: But I tell you, miss, it’s of all the consequence in the world. I would not lose the rest of it for a guinea. Here, mother, do you make it out. Of no consequence!

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: How’s this?— “Dear ’Squire, I’m now waiting for Miss Neville, with a post-chaise and pair, at the bottom of the garden, but I find my horses yet unable to perform the journey. I expect you’ll assist us with a pair of fresh horses, as you promised. Dispatch is necessary, as the HAG (ay, the hag), your mother, will otherwise suspect us! Yours, Hastings.” Grant me patience. I shall run distracted! My rage chokes me.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I hope, madam, you’ll suspend your resentment for a few moments, and not impute to me any impertinence, or sinister design, that belongs to another.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Fine spoken, madam, you are most miraculously polite and engaging, and quite the very pink of courtesy and circumspection, madam. And you, you great ill-fashioned oaf, with scarce sense enough to keep your mouth shut: were you, too, joined against me? But I’ll defeat all your plots in a moment. As for you, madam, since you have got a pair of fresh horses ready, it would be cruel to disappoint them. So, if you please, instead of running away with your spark, prepare, this very moment, to run off with ME. Your old aunt Pedigree will keep you secure, I’ll warrant me. You too, sir, may mount your horse, and guard us upon the way. Here, Thomas, Roger, Diggory! I’ll show you, that I wish you better than you do yourselves.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: So now I’m completely ruined.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ay, that’s a sure thing.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: What better could be expected from being connected with such a stupid fool,—and after all the nods and signs I made him?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: By the laws, miss, it was your own cleverness, and not my stupidity, that did your business. You were so nice and so busy with your Shake-bags and Goose-greens, that I thought you could never be making believe.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: So, sir, I find by my servant, that you have shown my letter, and betrayed us. Was this well done, young gentleman?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Here’s another. Ask miss there, who betrayed you. Ecod, it was her doing, not mine.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: So I have been finely used here among you. Rendered contemptible, driven into ill manners, despised, insulted, laughed at.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Here’s another. We shall have old Bedlam broke loose presently.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: And there, sir, is the gentleman to whom we all owe every obligation.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: What can I say to him, a mere boy, an idiot, whose ignorance and age are a protection?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: A poor contemptible booby, that would but disgrace correction.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Yet with cunning and malice enough to make himself merry with all our embarrassments.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: An insensible cub.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Replete with tricks and mischief.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Baw! damme, but I’ll fight you both, one after the other——with baskets.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: As for him, he’s below resentment. But your conduct, Mr. Hastings, requires an explanation. You knew of my mistakes, yet would not undeceive me.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Tortured as I am with my own disappointments, is this a time for explanations? It is not friendly, Mr. Marlow.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: But, sir——

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Mr. Marlow, we never kept on your mistake till it was too late to undeceive you.

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
speeches.text: My mistress desires you’ll get ready immediately, madam. The horses are putting to. Your hat and things are in the next room. We are to go thirty miles before morning.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Well, well: I’ll come presently.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Was it well done, sir, to assist in rendering me ridiculous? To hang me out for the scorn of all my acquaintance? Depend upon it, sir, I shall expect an explanation.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Was it well done, sir, if you’re upon that subject, to deliver what I entrusted to yourself, to the care of another sir?

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Mr. Hastings! Mr. Marlow! Why will you increase my distress by this groundless dispute? I implore, I entreat you——

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
speeches.text: Your cloak, madam. My mistress is impatient.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I come. Pray be pacified. If I leave you thus, I shall die with apprehension.

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
speeches.text: Your fan, muff, and gloves, madam. The horses are waiting.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: O, Mr. Marlow! if you knew what a scene of constraint and ill-nature lies before me, I’m sure it would convert your resentment into pity.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I’m so distracted with a variety of passions, that I don’t know what I do. Forgive me, madam. George, forgive me. You know my hasty temper, and should not exasperate it.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: The torture of my situation is my only excuse.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Well, my dear Hastings, if you have that esteem for me that I think, that I am sure you have, your constancy for three years will but increase the happiness of our future connexion. If——

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Miss Neville. Constance, why Constance, I say.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I’m coming. Well, constancy, remember, constancy is the word.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: My heart! how can I support this? To be so near happiness, and such happiness!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: You see now, young gentleman, the effects of your folly. What might be amusement to you, is here disappointment, and even distress.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ecod, I have hit it. It’s here. Your hands. Yours and yours, my poor Sulky!—My boots there, ho!—Meet me two hours hence at the bottom of the garden; and if you don’t find Tony Lumpkin a more good-natured fellow than you thought for, I’ll give you leave to take my best horse, and Bet Bouncer into the bargain. Come along. My boots, ho!

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: You saw the old lady and Miss Neville drive off, you say?

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
speeches.text: Yes, your honour. They went off in a post-coach, and the young ’squire went on horseback. They’re thirty miles off by this time.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Then all my hopes are over.

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
speeches.text: Yes, sir. Old Sir Charles has arrived. He and the old gentleman of the house have been laughing at Mr. Marlow’s mistake this half hour. They are coming this way.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Then I must not be seen. So now to my fruitless appointment at the bottom of the garden. This is about the time.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ha! ha! ha! The peremptory tone in which he sent forth his sublime commands!

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: And the reserve with which I suppose he treated all your advances.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And yet he might have seen something in me above a common innkeeper, too.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: Yes, Dick, but he mistook you for an uncommon innkeeper, ha! ha! ha!

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, I’m in too good spirits to think of anything but joy. Yes, my dear friend, this union of our families will make our personal friendships hereditary; and though my daughter’s fortune is but small—

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: Why, Dick, will you talk of fortune to ME? My son is possessed of more than a competence already, and can want nothing but a good and virtuous girl to share his happiness and increase it. If they like each other, as you say they do—

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: IF, man! I tell you they DO like each other. My daughter as good as told me so.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: But girls are apt to flatter themselves, you know.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I saw him grasp her hand in the warmest manner myself; and here he comes to put you out of your IFS, I warrant him.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I come, sir, once more, to ask pardon for my strange conduct. I can scarce reflect on my insolence without confusion.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Tut, boy, a trifle! You take it too gravely. An hour or two’s laughing with my daughter will set all to rights again. She’ll never like you the worse for it.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Sir, I shall be always proud of her approbation.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Approbation is but a cold word, Mr. Marlow; if I am not deceived, you have something more than approbation thereabouts. You take me?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Really, sir, I have not that happiness.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Come, boy, I’m an old fellow, and know what’s what as well as you that are younger. I know what has passed between you; but mum.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Sure, sir, nothing has passed between us but the most profound respect on my side, and the most distant reserve on hers. You don’t think, sir, that my impudence has been passed upon all the rest of the family.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Impudence! No, I don’t say that—not quite impudence—though girls like to be played with, and rumpled a little too, sometimes. But she has told no tales, I assure you.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I never gave her the slightest cause.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, well, I like modesty in its place well enough. But this is over-acting, young gentleman. You may be open. Your father and I will like you all the better for it.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: May I die, sir, if I ever——

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I tell you, she don’t dislike you; and as I’m sure you like her——

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Dear sir—I protest, sir——

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I see no reason why you should not be joined as fast as the parson can tie you.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: But hear me, sir—

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Your father approves the match, I admire it; every moment’s delay will be doing mischief. So—

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: But why won’t you hear me? By all that’s just and true, I never gave Miss Hardcastle the slightest mark of my attachment, or even the most distant hint to suspect me of affection. We had but one interview, and that was formal, modest, and uninteresting.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: This fellow’s formal modest impudence is beyond bearing.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: And you never grasped her hand, or made any protestations?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: As Heaven is my witness, I came down in obedience to your commands. I saw the lady without emotion, and parted without reluctance. I hope you’ll exact no farther proofs of my duty, nor prevent me from leaving a house in which I suffer so many mortifications.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: I’m astonished at the air of sincerity with which he parted.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And I’m astonished at the deliberate intrepidity of his assurance.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: I dare pledge my life and honour upon his truth.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Here comes my daughter, and I would stake my happiness upon her veracity.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Kate, come hither, child. Answer us sincerely and without reserve: has Mr. Marlow made you any professions of love and affection?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: The question is very abrupt, sir. But since you require unreserved sincerity, I think he has.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You see.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: And pray, madam, have you and my son had more than one interview?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Yes, sir, several.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: You see.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: But did be profess any attachment?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: A lasting one.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: Did he talk of love?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Much, sir.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: Amazing! And all this formally?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Formally.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Now, my friend, I hope you are satisfied.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: And how did he behave, madam?

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: As most profest admirers do: said some civil things of my face, talked much of his want of merit, and the greatness of mine; mentioned his heart, gave a short tragedy speech, and ended with pretended rapture.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: Now I’m perfectly convinced, indeed. I know his conversation among women to be modest and submissive: this forward canting ranting manner by no means describes him; and, I am confident, he never sat for the picture.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Then, what, sir, if I should convince you to your face of my sincerity? If you and my papa, in about half an hour, will place yourselves behind that screen, you shall hear him declare his passion to me in person.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: Agreed. And if I find him what you describe, all my happiness in him must have an end.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And if you don’t find him what I describe—I fear my happiness must never have a beginning.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: What an idiot am I, to wait here for a fellow who probably takes a delight in mortifying me. He never intended to be punctual, and I’ll wait no longer. What do I see? It is he! and perhaps with news of my Constance.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: My honest ’squire! I now find you a man of your word. This looks like friendship.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ay, I’m your friend, and the best friend you have in the world, if you knew but all. This riding by night, by the bye, is cursedly tiresome. It has shook me worse than the basket of a stage-coach.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But how? where did you leave your fellow-travellers? Are they in safety? Are they housed?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Five and twenty miles in two hours and a half is no such bad driving. The poor beasts have smoked for it: rabbit me, but I’d rather ride forty miles after a fox than ten with such varment.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Well, but where have you left the ladies? I die with impatience.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Left them! Why where should I leave them but where I found them?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: This is a riddle.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Riddle me this then. What’s that goes round the house, and round the house, and never touches the house?

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: I’m still astray.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Why, that’s it, mon. I have led them astray. By jingo, there’s not a pond or a slough within five miles of the place but they can tell the taste of.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Ha! ha! ha! I understand: you took them in a round, while they supposed themselves going forward, and so you have at last brought them home again.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: You shall hear. I first took them down Feather-bed Lane, where we stuck fast in the mud. I then rattled them crack over the stones of Up-and-down Hill. I then introduced them to the gibbet on Heavy-tree Heath; and from that, with a circumbendibus, I fairly lodged them in the horse-pond at the bottom of the garden.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But no accident, I hope?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: No, no. Only mother is confoundedly frightened. She thinks herself forty miles off. She’s sick of the journey; and the cattle can scarce crawl. So if your own horses be ready, you may whip off with cousin, and I’ll be bound that no soul here can budge a foot to follow you.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: My dear friend, how can I be grateful?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ay, now it’s dear friend, noble ’squire. Just now, it was all idiot, cub, and run me through the guts. Damn YOUR way of fighting, I say. After we take a knock in this part of the country, we kiss and be friends. But if you had run me through the guts, then I should be dead, and you might go kiss the hangman.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: The rebuke is just. But I must hasten to relieve Miss Neville: if you keep the old lady employed, I promise to take care of the young one.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Never fear me. Here she comes. Vanish. She’s got from the pond, and draggled up to the waist like a mermaid.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Oh, Tony, I’m killed! Shook! Battered to death. I shall never survive it. That last jolt, that laid us against the quickset hedge, has done my business.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Alack, mamma, it was all your own fault. You would be for running away by night, without knowing one inch of the way.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I wish we were at home again. I never met so many accidents in so short a journey. Drenched in the mud, overturned in a ditch, stuck fast in a slough, jolted to a jelly, and at last to lose our way. Whereabouts do you think we are, Tony?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: By my guess we should come upon Crackskull Common, about forty miles from home.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: O lud! O lud! The most notorious spot in all the country. We only want a robbery to make a complete night on’t.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Don’t be afraid, mamma, don’t be afraid. Two of the five that kept here are hanged, and the other three may not find us. Don’t be afraid.—Is that a man that’s galloping behind us? No; it’s only a tree.—Don’t be afraid.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: The fright will certainly kill me.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Do you see anything like a black hat moving behind the thicket?

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Oh, death!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: No; it’s only a cow. Don’t be afraid, mamma; don’t be afraid.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: As I’m alive, Tony, I see a man coming towards us. Ah! I’m sure on’t. If he perceives us, we are undone.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Father-in-law, by all that’s unlucky, come to take one of his night walks. Ah, it’s a highwayman with pistols as long as my arm. A damned ill-looking fellow.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Good Heaven defend us! He approaches.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Do you hide yourself in that thicket, and leave me to manage him. If there be any danger, I’ll cough, and cry hem. When I cough, be sure to keep close.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I’m mistaken, or I heard voices of people in want of help. Oh, Tony! is that you? I did not expect you so soon back. Are your mother and her charge in safety?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Very safe, sir, at my aunt Pedigree’s. Hem.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ah, death! I find there’s danger.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Forty miles in three hours; sure that’s too much, my youngster.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Stout horses and willing minds make short journeys, as they say. Hem.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Sure he’ll do the dear boy no harm.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: But I heard a voice here; I should be glad to know from whence it came.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: It was I, sir, talking to myself, sir. I was saying that forty miles in four hours was very good going. Hem. As to be sure it was. Hem. I have got a sort of cold by being out in the air. We’ll go in, if you please. Hem.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: But if you talked to yourself you did not answer yourself. I’m certain I heard two voices, and am resolved to find the other out.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Oh! he’s coming to find me out. Oh!

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: What need you go, sir, if I tell you? Hem. I’ll lay down my life for the truth—hem—I’ll tell you all, sir.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I tell you I will not be detained. I insist on seeing. It’s in vain to expect I’ll believe you.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: O lud! he’ll murder my poor boy, my darling! Here, good gentleman, whet your rage upon me. Take my money, my life, but spare that young gentleman; spare my child, if you have any mercy.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: My wife, as I’m a Christian. From whence can she come? or what does she mean?

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Take compassion on us, good Mr. Highwayman. Take our money, our watches, all we have, but spare our lives. We will never bring you to justice; indeed we won’t, good Mr. Highwayman.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I believe the woman’s out of her senses. What, Dorothy, don’t you know ME?

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Mr. Hardcastle, as I’m alive! My fears blinded me. But who, my dear, could have expected to meet you here, in this frightful place, so far from home? What has brought you to follow us?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Sure, Dorothy, you have not lost your wits? So far from home, when you are within forty yards of your own door! This is one of your old tricks, you graceless rogue, you. Don’t you know the gate, and the mulberry-tree; and don’t you remember the horse-pond, my dear?

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Yes, I shall remember the horse-pond as long as I live; I have caught my death in it. And it is to you, you graceless varlet, I owe all this? I’ll teach you to abuse your mother, I will.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Ecod, mother, all the parish says you have spoiled me, and so you may take the fruits on’t.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I’ll spoil you, I will.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: There’s morality, however, in his reply.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: My dear Constance, why will you deliberate thus? If we delay a moment, all is lost for ever. Pluck up a little resolution, and we shall soon be out of the reach of her malignity.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: I find it impossible. My spirits are so sunk with the agitations I have suffered, that I am unable to face any new danger. Two or three years’ patience will at last crown us with happiness.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Such a tedious delay is worse than inconstancy. Let us fly, my charmer. Let us date our happiness from this very moment. Perish fortune! Love and content will increase what we possess beyond a monarch’s revenue. Let me prevail!

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: No, Mr. Hastings, no. Prudence once more comes to my relief, and I will obey its dictates. In the moment of passion fortune may be despised, but it ever produces a lasting repentance. I’m resolved to apply to Mr. Hardcastle’s compassion and justice for redress.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: But though he had the will, he has not the power to relieve you.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: But he has influence, and upon that I am resolved to rely.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: I have no hopes. But since you persist, I must reluctantly obey you.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: What a situation am I in! If what you say appears, I shall then find a guilty son. If what he says be true, I shall then lose one that, of all others, I most wished for a daughter.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I am proud of your approbation, and to show I merit it, if you place yourselves as I directed, you shall hear his explicit declaration. But he comes.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: I’ll to your father, and keep him to the appointment.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Though prepared for setting out, I come once more to take leave; nor did I, till this moment, know the pain I feel in the separation.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I believe sufferings cannot be very great, sir, which you can so easily remove. A day or two longer, perhaps, might lessen your uneasiness, by showing the little value of what you now think proper to regret.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: This girl every moment improves upon me. It must not be, madam. I have already trifled too long with my heart. My very pride begins to submit to my passion. The disparity of education and fortune, the anger of a parent, and the contempt of my equals, begin to lose their weight; and nothing can restore me to myself but this painful effort of resolution.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Then go, sir: I’ll urge nothing more to detain you. Though my family be as good as hers you came down to visit, and my education, I hope, not inferior, what are these advantages without equal affluence? I must remain contented with the slight approbation of imputed merit; I must have only the mockery of your addresses, while all your serious aims are fixed on fortune.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: Here, behind this screen.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, ay; make no noise. I’ll engage my Kate covers him with confusion at last.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: By heavens, madam! fortune was ever my smallest consideration. Your beauty at first caught my eye; for who could see that without emotion? But every moment that I converse with you steals in some new grace, heightens the picture, and gives it stronger expression. What at first seemed rustic plainness, now appears refined simplicity. What seemed forward assurance, now strikes me as the result of courageous innocence and conscious virtue.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: What can it mean? He amazes me!

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: I told you how it would be. Hush!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: I am now determined to stay, madam; and I have too good an opinion of my father’s discernment, when he sees you, to doubt his approbation.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: No, Mr. Marlow, I will not, cannot detain you. Do you think I could suffer a connexion in which there is the smallest room for repentance? Do you think I would take the mean advantage of a transient passion, to load you with confusion? Do you think I could ever relish that happiness which was acquired by lessening yours?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: By all that’s good, I can have no happiness but what’s in your power to grant me! Nor shall I ever feel repentance but in not having seen your merits before. I will stay even contrary to your wishes; and though you should persist to shun me, I will make my respectful assiduities atone for the levity of my past conduct.

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Sir, I must entreat you’ll desist. As our acquaintance began, so let it end, in indifference. I might have given an hour or two to levity; but seriously, Mr. Marlow, do you think I could ever submit to a connexion where I must appear mercenary, and you imprudent? Do you think I could ever catch at the confident addresses of a secure admirer?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Does this look like security? Does this look like confidence? No, madam, every moment that shows me your merit, only serves to increase my diffidence and confusion. Here let me continue——

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: I can hold it no longer. Charles, Charles, how hast thou deceived me! Is this your indifference, your uninteresting conversation?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Your cold contempt; your formal interview! What have you to say now?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: That I’m all amazement! What can it mean?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: It means that you can say and unsay things at pleasure: that you can address a lady in private, and deny it in public: that you have one story for us, and another for my daughter.

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Daughter!—This lady your daughter?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Yes, sir, my only daughter; my Kate; whose else should she be?

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Oh, the devil!

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Yes, sir, that very identical tall squinting lady you were pleased to take me for; she that you addressed as the mild, modest, sentimental man of gravity, and the bold, forward, agreeable Rattle of the Ladies’ Club. Ha! ha! ha!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Zounds! there’s no bearing this; it’s worse than death!

speeches.speaker: MISS HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: In which of your characters, sir, will you give us leave to address you? As the faltering gentleman, with looks on the ground, that speaks just to be heard, and hates hypocrisy; or the loud confident creature, that keeps it up with Mrs. Mantrap, and old Miss Biddy Buckskin, till three in the morning? Ha! ha! ha!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: O, curse on my noisy head. I never attempted to be impudent yet, that I was not taken down. I must be gone.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: By the hand of my body, but you shall not. I see it was all a mistake, and I am rejoiced to find it. You shall not, sir, I tell you. I know she’ll forgive you. Won’t you forgive him, Kate? We’ll all forgive you. Take courage, man.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: So, so, they’re gone off. Let them go, I care not.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Who gone?

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: My dutiful niece and her gentleman, Mr. Hastings, from town. He who came down with our modest visitor here.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: Who, my honest George Hastings? As worthy a fellow as lives, and the girl could not have made a more prudent choice.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Then, by the hand of my body, I’m proud of the connexion.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Well, if he has taken away the lady, he has not taken her fortune; that remains in this family to console us for her loss.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Sure, Dorothy, you would not be so mercenary?

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, that’s my affair, not yours.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: But you know if your son, when of age, refuses to marry his cousin, her whole fortune is then at her own disposal.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Ay, but he’s not of age, and she has not thought proper to wait for his refusal.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: What, returned so soon! I begin not to like it.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: For my late attempt to fly off with your niece let my present confusion be my punishment. We are now come back, to appeal from your justice to your humanity. By her father’s consent, I first paid her my addresses, and our passions were first founded in duty.

speeches.speaker: MISS NEVILLE
speeches.text: Since his death, I have been obliged to stoop to dissimulation to avoid oppression. In an hour of levity, I was ready to give up my fortune to secure my choice. But I am now recovered from the delusion, and hope from your tenderness what is denied me from a nearer connexion.

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Pshaw, pshaw! this is all but the whining end of a modern novel.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Be it what it will, I’m glad they’re come back to reclaim their due. Come hither, Tony, boy. Do you refuse this lady’s hand whom I now offer you?

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: What signifies my refusing? You know I can’t refuse her till I’m of age, father.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: While I thought concealing your age, boy, was likely to conduce to your improvement, I concurred with your mother’s desire to keep it secret. But since I find she turns it to a wrong use, I must now declare you have been of age these three months.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Of age! Am I of age, father?

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: Above three months.

speeches.speaker: TONY
speeches.text: Then you’ll see the first use I’ll make of my liberty. Witness all men by these presents, that I, Anthony Lumpkin, Esquire, of BLANK place, refuse you, Constantia Neville, spinster, of no place at all, for my true and lawful wife. So Constance Neville may marry whom she pleases, and Tony Lumpkin is his own man again.

speeches.speaker: SIR CHARLES
speeches.text: O brave ’squire!

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: My worthy friend!

speeches.speaker: MRS. HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: My undutiful offspring!

speeches.speaker: MARLOW
speeches.text: Joy, my dear George! I give you joy sincerely. And could I prevail upon my little tyrant here to be less arbitrary, I should be the happiest man alive, if you would return me the favour.

speeches.speaker: HASTINGS
speeches.text: Come, madam, you are now driven to the very last scene of all your contrivances. I know you like him, I’m sure he loves you, and you must and shall have him.

speeches.speaker: HARDCASTLE
speeches.text: And I say so too. And, Mr. Marlow, if she makes as good a wife as she has a daughter, I don’t believe you’ll ever repent your bargain. So now to supper. To-morrow we shall gather all the poor of the parish about us, and the mistakes of the night shall be crowned with a merry morning. So, boy, take her; and as you have been mistaken in the mistress, my wish is, that you may never be mistaken in the wife.
